food.text: Kabsa is a mixed rice dish that originates from Yemen. It is commonly regarded as a national dish in all the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. It can also be found in southern Iran, Gaza and the Malabar Coast of India.

According to the Saudi Arabian Cultural Mission, serving gahwah (coffee) in Saudi Arabia is a sign of hospitality and generosity. Traditionally, the beans were roasted, cooled and ground with a mortar and pestle in front of the guests. The host added cardamom pods during the grinding.

Dates are associated in Saudi Arabia with the tradition of breaking the fast after Ramadan. Most food ingredients there, such as wheat, dates, ghee, meat, fish and vegetables, are sourced locally. Serving dishes to guests is a way of expressing generosity.

Today gahwah is no longer prepared in front of the guests. It is served in a dallah and poured into small cups called finjan. Traditional coffeehouses (maqha) used to be ubiquitous, but are now being displaced by food-hall-style cafes.

Eastern Arabian cooking uses many of the same spices as Indian cuisine. This is partly the result of heavy trading between the two regions. It also reflects the wealthy oil states, in which many South Asian workers live abroad in Eastern Arabia.

Turkic people arrived in Mecca in the early 20th century, most for Hajj or to escape the Russian Empire. They left a significant mark on Saudi cuisine. Many Central Asian dishes became staples, such as Bukhari rice, dumplings, laghman and manti.

In January 2024, the Saudi Culinary Commission, which operates under the Ministry of Culture, announced the regional dishes of Saudi Arabia's 13 regions. It was a formal effort to name the food identity of each part of the country.

The Bedouins of the Arabian Peninsula rely on a diet of dates, dried fruit, nuts, wheat, barley, rice and meat. The meat comes from large animals such as cows, camels, goats, sheep and lambs. They also eat dairy products including milk, cheese, yoghurt and buttermilk (labneh).

In eastern Arabia, Arabic coffee, known locally as qahwa, is served in an ornately crafted dallah and poured into a small cup called a finjaan. It symbolizes warmth and respect and is often served alongside dates. Hosts keep refilling the finjaan until the guest gently shakes the cup to signal they have had enough.

Sobia is a cold drink usually made in the Hijaz but now available all over Saudi Arabia, especially during Ramadan. It is made from a light fermented mixture of barley or brown bread, date palm sap, herbs and spices. It may be white or colored depending on the flavor.

art.text: Modern Saudi fine art traces its start to the 1950s. In 1953 the artist Abdulhalim Radwi showed some of his early artworks at the first exhibition of school-based activities in the history of public education. In 1958 King Saud bin Abdulaziz inaugurated Saudi Arabia's first art exhibition, organized by the Ministry of Knowledge.

For centuries before modern fine art arrived, Arabic calligraphy and handicrafts were the only forms of visual art commonly practiced in the societies of the Arabian Peninsula. Handicrafts appeared in everyday objects such as ornaments, housewares, decoration and clothing, and could commonly be found in local markets.

Public schooling gave Saudi art an early boost. Early public education is often credited with encouraging the art of drawing, even though artistic tools were scarce. This helped lay the ground for the modern art scene that followed.

Arabic calligraphy held a highly symbolic position because of its link to transcribing the Quran. Its firm traditions went beyond local practice, and the craft was passed on from generation to generation through the Ijazah.

The Ministry of Knowledge decided to introduce painting and fine arts as school subjects, in the boys' curriculum in 1957 and the girls' curriculum in 1959. This decision laid the foundation for fine arts education in Saudi Arabia.

From 1954 to 1964, intensive summer training workshops were held for art teachers. They were led by a group of Arab artists alongside Saudi artists such as Abdul Halim Radawi, who taught across many of the courses.

Safeya Binzagr and Mounirah Mosly held their first joint exhibition in 1968 at the Dar Al-Tarbiyyah Al-Hadeethah School in Jeddah. Their show reflected the strong female presence in the trailblazing generation of Saudi artists.
Abdul Halim Radawi studied on a Ministry of Knowledge scholarship at the Accademia di Belle Arti di Roma in the 1960s. After graduating he taught across many of the art teacher training courses.
tags: Accademia di Belle Arti di Roma

art.text: Ministry of Knowledge scholarships sent several future pioneers abroad, including Muhammad Al-Saleem, Muhammad Al-Saqa'bi, Dia Aziz and Ahmad Felemban. Through solo and group art shows, they represented the avant-garde of modern art in Saudi Arabia.
Early solo shows spread beyond one city. Abdul Aziz Al-Hammad held his first exhibition at Dammam's Fifth School in 1966, and Muhammad Al-Saleem exhibited at Riyadh's Al Nassr Club in 1967.

The new art scene also produced art journalism. Artists such as Abduljabbar Al Yahya, Abdulrahman Al-Suleiman and Muhammad Al-Monif wrote about fine arts in the supplements of cultural newspapers or on dedicated pages.

war.text: On 13 January 1902, Ibn Saud captured the walled city of Riyadh from the Rashidi dynasty. The battle is widely regarded as the starting point of the Saudi unification campaigns, which ended with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia being established in 1932.

The unification of Saudi Arabia was a series of military and political campaigns that began in 1902 and culminated in 1932. Ibn Saud subjugated the rest of Najd, seized Al-Hasa from the Ottoman Empire, and conquered Jabal Shammar and the Hejaz between 1913 and 1925. It has often been claimed that the process caused some 400,000 to 800,000 casualties. Recent research suggests that, though bloody, the number of deaths and injuries was significantly lower.

In 1934 Saudi Arabia and the Kingdom of Yemen went to war after Yemen's Imam Yahya seized highland townships. The Saudis advanced quickly with the help of British planes, while the Yemenis were fighting with swords. Saudi forces captured Hajara and Najran in April.

The Battle of Khafji, from 29 January to 1 February 1991, was the first major ground engagement of the Gulf War. Iraqi divisions invaded Saudi Arabia, and one column occupied the city of Khafji on the night of 29–30 January. Saudi National Guard battalions and Qatari tank companies retook it with Coalition air and artillery support, at the cost of 43 Coalition servicemen dead and 52 wounded. Iraqi dead are put between 60 and 300, and an estimated 400 were captured.

After the 2026 Iran war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, Iran launched retaliatory missile strikes on locations across Saudi Arabia. On 1 March Saudi Arabia intercepted missiles aimed at Prince Sultan Air Base and the Riyadh airport without any material losses, but an Iranian missile attack on a US base in Saudi Arabia left a US soldier who died of his injuries eight days later. On 2 March Saudi Arabia claimed to have intercepted two drones aimed at the Ras Tanura oil refinery, though falling shrapnel started a limited fire.
war.source_title: Saudi Arabia in the 2026 Iran war

war.text: The Saudi conquest of the Hashemite Kingdom of Hejaz took place in 1924 and 1925, and ended in December 1925 with the fall of Jeddah. In 1926 Abdulaziz was proclaimed king of Hejaz, and he raised Nejd to a kingdom in 1927.

After Iraq invaded Kuwait, Saudi Arabia feared it would be next and requested immediate military aid. The Coalition first deployed over 200,000 soldiers, 750 aircraft and 1,200 tanks in Saudi Arabia. This quickly grew to 3,600 tanks and over 600,000 personnel, of whom over 500,000 were from the United States.

During the 1934 war with Saudi Arabia, Imam Yahya announced a bold plan to advance on Riyadh with 200,000 men, but the attack never eventuated. Reports from the war were contradictory by 10 May, and one data guide says the Saudis decisively won on 13 May 1934.

In January 1991, Iraq tried to deter Coalition action by threatening Kuwait's and Iraq's oil. On 16 January Iraqi artillery destroyed an oil storage tank in Khafji, and on 19 January the pumps at the Ahmadi loading complex were opened, pouring crude oil into the Persian Gulf at 200,000 barrels a day. It became one of the worst ecological disasters to that date.

Historians disagreed about whether European rivalry lay behind the 1934 Saudi–Yemeni conflict. Alexei Vasiliev wrote in 1998 that Italians encouraged the imam to increase their influence in Yemen, and that the British wished to distract him from their protectorates in Aden. The war ended with a treaty signed in Taif.

literature.text: The first book in the history of Saudi Arabia was published in 1925, when the Saudi era began in the Hijaz. It was Mohammed bin Suroor Sabban's Literature of the Hijaz. It appeared amid a modern literary movement, new printing technology and the influence of wider Arab literary movements.

Saudi literary works face pervasive censorship. Even after reforms allowed some previously banned books at the Riyadh Book Fair, the Ministry of Media still keeps a list of banned works. It includes Cities of Salt by Abdul Rahman Munif, works by Mahmoud Darwish and the Harry Potter series.

Nabati is a vernacular Arabic poetry from the Arabian Peninsula, composed in colloquial Arabic rather than by classical rules. It was once used to declare war, seek peace and resolve tribal disputes. It lapsed after the discovery of oil and the region's development, but has enjoyed a considerable renaissance, especially in the UAE.

In 1926 the Hijazi Library, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's first publishing house, published a second book by Mohammed Suroor Sabban. It was titled The Exhibition (Al-Ma'rad). The Hijaz was the center of early Saudi publishing.

Soon after the Saudi state was founded in the early twentieth century, Saudi literature was born. The Najdi poet Muhammad bin Abdullah bin Uthaymin was a prominent pioneer who brought about a renaissance in poetic style. Literary figures also emerged in Al-Ahsa and Qatif in the east of the Kingdom.

Saudi literary publishing grew from 409 books in 2014 to 701 books in 2022. It then fell to 523 books in 2023 and 509 in 2024, the lowest level since 2018. The Report on the State of Culture in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia 2024 noted that 2024 was even lower than 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic.
tags: Report on the State of Culture in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia 2024

literature.text: Nabati poetry is now a celebrated medium of both poetry and song in the UAE. One of its largest competitions, Million's Poet, has been held biannually since 2006 and is broadcast as a reality TV show. Practitioners such as Ousha bint Khalifa Al Suwaidi, known as Fatat Al Arab, have become celebrated figures.
Wilfred Thesiger's Arabian Sands, published in 1959, is a classic of travel writing about the Bedouin. A British adventurer, Thesiger lived as and with the Bedu of the Empty Quarter for five years.

Muhammad Hassan Awwad published Avowed Thoughts (Khawatir Musarrahah) in 1926. That made him the first Saudi writer to produce an independent literary work. Classical poetry was the dominant literary form in this early period.

Saudi novels followed a different path from overall literary output. The number of novels by Saudi authors rose from 161 in 2019 to 201 in 2020, dipped to 155 in 2021, then jumped to 208 in 2022. After 182 in 2023, the total reached 218 in 2024, an increase of nearly 20% on the previous year.
tags: Report on the State of Culture in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia 2024

literature.text: The Heera group of nabati poets grew up as close friends in the village of Al Heera in Sharjah. The three were Khalfan Musabah (1923 to 1946), Sheikh Saqr Al Qasimi (1925 to 1993), a former ruler of Sharjah, and Sultan bin Ali Al Owais (1925 to 2000).

The Harry Potter series is among the books on the Saudi Ministry of Media's banned list. The series was banned because it was said to contain "occult or satanic theme, violence and anti-family" messages.

science.text: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) was founded in 2009 in Thuwal, Saudi Arabia. It offers research and graduate programs taught in English. It was also the first mixed-gender university campus in the country.
science.source_title: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

science.text: The Arabian oryx was hunted to extinction in the wild by 1972. Zoos and private reserves kept the species alive, and by 1980 enough oryxes lived in captivity for reintroduction to begin. The first release was in Oman, using animals from the San Diego Wild Animal Park.

KAUST's campus was Saudi Arabia's first LEED certified project and is the world's largest LEED Platinum campus. Designed by Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum, it includes wind towers and solar panels. It was named one of the 2010 Top Ten Green Projects by the American Institute of Architects committee on the environment.
science.source_title: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

science.text: In 1988 KACST began planning to develop nuclear technology in Saudi Arabia and opened the Atomic Energy Research Institute (AERI). The institute has four departments: Radiation Protection, Industrial Applications, Nuclear Reactors and Safety, and Materials.
science.source_title: King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology

science.text: KACST's Space Research Institute has designed satellites for scientific purposes, including SaudiSat 5A and 5B, SaudiComSat-1 and SaudiGeo-1. The list also includes Arabsat-6A, which was launched on 4 February 2019.
science.source_title: King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology

science.text: In the 1930s, Arabian princes and oil company clerks started hunting Arabian oryxes with automobiles and rifles. The hunts grew in size, and some were reported to employ as many as 300 vehicles. By the middle of the 20th century the northern population was effectively extinct, and the last Arabian oryx in the wild before reintroduction was reported in 1972.

The Arabian oryx was classified as endangered on the IUCN Red List in 1986. In 2011 it became the first animal to revert to vulnerable status after previously being listed as extinct in the wild. It is listed in CITES Appendix I.

KAUST rose quickly in research rankings. In the 2016 Nature Index Rising Stars it ranked 19th in the world among the fastest rising universities. In 2025 Times Higher Education ranked it first among Arab universities for the third consecutive year.
science.source_title: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

science.text: In 2012 KACST announced Saudi Arabia's first electrostatic accelerator, designed by the National Center of Mathematics and Physics. In April 2013 it announced WaferCatalyst, an initiative to promote integrated circuit design in Saudi Arabia and surrounding regions.
science.source_title: King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology

science.text: In Saudi Arabia, one of the largest Arabian oryx populations lives in the Mahazat as-Sayd Protected Area, a fenced reserve of more than 2,000 km2. The 'Uruq Bani Ma'arid Protected Area held 116 oryxes as of 2024, up from 81 in 2020.

In June 2007, Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary became the first site ever removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List, because the Omani government decided to open 90% of it to oil prospecting. The site's Arabian oryx population had been reduced from 450 in 1996 to only 65 in 2007. By then, fewer than four breeding pairs were left on the site.

politics.text: Abdulaziz bin Abdul Rahman, known as Ibn Saud, founded the modern Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. From 1902 until his death in 1953, he ruled a succession of states, from the Emirate of Riyadh to the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd, before becoming King of Saudi Arabia.

In 1916, Hussein bin Ali, the Sharif of Mecca, started a pan-Arab revolt against Ottoman rule, backed by British encouragement and support. He aimed to establish a unified Arab state. The Allied victory in World War I ended Ottoman control in Arabia.

The Rashidi dynasty ruled the Emirate of Ha'il and was the most formidable enemy of the House of Saud. Its succession disputes, over whether power passed to a brother or a son, were often resolved violently, and six Rashidi leaders died violently in the last years of the 19th century. In the first two decades of the 20th century the Saudis and their allies fought a long series of wars to unite the peninsula, and by 1921 Abdulaziz Al Saud had captured Ha'il.

In January 1902, Ibn Saud reached Riyadh with around 40 men, having been given horses and arms by the Emir of Kuwait. He believed the only way to take the city was to capture Masmak fort and kill Ibn Ajlan, the chief of Riyadh. They achieved both and seized the city in a night raid. The House of Saud had been in exile since 1893, after the Rashidi dynasty removed them from power for the second time and dissolved their polity.

When civil war broke out in Yemen in 1962, Egyptian forces entered to support the new republican government while Saudi Arabia backed the royalists. Between 1962 and 1970, the Saudi monarchy faced one of the gravest threats to its survival from Yemen.

In 1995, Fahd suffered a debilitating stroke, and his half-brother Crown Prince Abdullah took over day-to-day government. Abdullah became king on Fahd's death in 2005. That December, after twelve years of talks, the World Trade Organization approved Saudi Arabia's membership.

Saudi Arabia has no national legislature elected by voters, and its Shura Council remains appointed. Qatar held a partial Shura Council election in 2021 with two thirds of seats elected, but in 2024 moved to abolish those elections and return to a fully appointed council.
politics.source_title: Arab states of the Persian Gulf

politics.text: Saud bin Abdulaziz was made emir of Ha'il at the age of 10 in 1910, and his maternal relatives of the Al Sabhan family ruled as regents. In 1920 he was assassinated by his cousin Abdullah bin Talal. Two of his widows then remarried: Norah bint Hammud Al Sabhan became Ibn Saud's eighth wife, and Fahda bint Asi bin Shuraim Al Shammari became his ninth wife and the mother of King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia.

In 1933, Yemen's Zaidi state, forged under Imam Muhammad bin Yahya Hamid ad-Din after the Ottoman Empire collapsed, came to blows with the Saudis over parts of Asir. The Saudis reached the port of Hodeidah before signing a treaty of Muslim friendship and Arab brotherhood in Taif. It was published simultaneously in Mecca, Sanaa, Damascus and Cairo to highlight its pan-Arabism.

In September 1962, the Freedom Officers led by Abdullah al-Sallal launched a coup in Sana to overthrow the Qasem dynasty and establish the Yemen Arab Republic. The royal family fled first to the mountains around Saada and then to Saudi Arabia. Eight years of civil war followed, with Nasser's United Arab Republic backing the republicans.

In 1975, King Faisal of Saudi Arabia was assassinated by his nephew, Faisal bin Musaid. Because the assassin's mother was a sister of Madawi al-Rasheed's father, the Saudi government accused the Rashidi family of being behind it. Further investigation found this untrue, but her family moved to Lebanon that year.

philosophy.text: In November 2020, the Saudi Philosophy Association was established as a non-profit, civil association concerned with the philosophical field in Saudi Arabia. It is described as the first philosophical association in the country.

Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri, born in Shaqra in Najd in 1938, is a Saudi polymath who has been called a theologian, jurist, historian, ethnographer, geographer, poet, critic and author. He belongs to Saudi Arabia's "Golden Generation," which knew both the poverty before the oil boom and the prosperity of the 1950s onward.
philosophy.source_title: Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri

philosophy.text: From the mid-1970s and 1980s, the international spread of Salafism and Wahhabism, favored by the conservative oil-exporting Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and other Gulf monarchies, reached a "preeminent position of strength in the global expression of Islam." The Saudi interpretation of Islam also included Islamist and revivalist strands, and a hybrid of the two until the 1990s.
philosophy.source_title: International propagation of the Salafi movement and Wahhabism

philosophy.text: Ibn Aqil hosted "Tafsir al-Tafasir," or "exegesis of the exegeses," a religious program broadcast daily on radio and weekly on television. He systematically collected all major explanations of the Qur'an within Sunni Islam and tried to integrate them, weighing the views of various theologians. The program was discontinued in the late 1980s, and he restarted it in 2010.
philosophy.source_title: Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri

philosophy.text: Ibn Aqil is a scholar of the Zahirite school of law within Sunni Islam and is described as the current era's primary biographer of the Zahirite theologian Ibn Hazm. His largest book on him, Nawadir al-Imam Ibn Hazm, collects Ibn Hazm's smaller, harder-to-find works, such as his poem on the fundamental principles of Zahirite law.
philosophy.source_title: Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri

philosophy.text: On 25 August 1988, at its 32nd session in Ta'if, the Board of Senior Ulema of Saudi Arabia issued a comprehensive fatwa condemning terrorism and recommending the death penalty for such acts. Its members included influential scholars such as Muhammad ibn al-Uthaymeen and Ibn Baz.
philosophy.source_title: International propagation of the Salafi movement and Wahhabism

philosophy.text: Ibn Aqil expressed skepticism about the goals and results of the Arab Spring. He considered the positions of Egyptian cleric Yusuf al-Qaradawi during the movement hypocritical and contradictory, charges which al-Qaradawi denied.
philosophy.source_title: Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri

philosophy.text: In 1998, Ibn Aqil delivered a lecture explaining Ibn Rushd's attempts to reconcile philosophy and religion. It was given at the International Averroes Symposium, co-sponsored by UNESCO in Carthage between 16 and 22 February.
philosophy.source_title: Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri

philosophy.text: In 2011, Ibn Aqil engaged in a public series of exchanges with fellow cleric Abdul-Rahman al-Barrak. The dispute arose because Ibn Aqil refused to adopt a formal position on the theological issues debated during the Mihna, a rare Medieval-era inquisition within Islam. In the Mihna, rationalists persecuted their orthodox counterparts.
philosophy.source_title: Abu Abd al-Rahman Ibn Aqil al-Zahiri

culture.text: Saudi Arabia was transformed from an impoverished Bedouin society into a rich commodity producer in just a few years in the 1970s. Its culture is still shaped by Arab and Islamic heritage, and society is generally religious, conservative, traditional and family-oriented.

Association football is the national sport of Saudi Arabia. Its national team reached a joint record six AFC Asian Cup finals, winning three of them in 1984, 1988 and 1996. In December 2024, Saudi Arabia was confirmed as host of the 2034 FIFA World Cup.

Lawrence of Arabia, a 1962 epic film directed by David Lean, depicts T. E. Lawrence's experiences in the Hejaz and Syria during the First World War. Its themes include Lawrence's emotional struggles with the violence inherent in war. In the film he must execute Gasim, he kills the wounded Farraj to save him from the Turks, who torture their captives, and he is captured, stripped, beaten and, it is implied, raped by the Turkish Bey at Deraa. The film also shows the Arabs massacring retreating Turkish soldiers who had just massacred the residents of Tafas. It won seven Oscars at the 35th Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest films ever made.

Legal chattel slavery existed in Saudi Arabia from antiquity until its formal abolition in 1962. In the 1930s, Saudi Arabia and the rest of the Arabian Peninsula was the main center of legal chattel slavery. Slaves were bought and sold in markets: many were children and young women trafficked from Africa, some lured on false pretenses such as pilgrimage, and female slaves were used as domestic servants or as concubines (sex slaves). Many members of the Afro-Saudi minority are descendants of the former slaves, and after abolition former slaves were often forced to rely on prostitution to survive.
Fierce religious resistance in Saudi Arabia had to be overcome to permit several innovations: paper money in 1951, the abolition of slavery in 1962, female education in 1964, and television in 1965.

When Abdulaziz's Ikhwan forces conquered the Hejaz by the end of 1925, they laid waste symbols of "heathen" practices around Mecca. The old cosmopolitan society of the Hejaz was uprooted, and a version of Wahhabi culture was imposed as a new compulsory social order.

Since 2023, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund has brought elite footballers such as Cristiano Ronaldo, Neymar, Sadio Mané and Jordan Henderson to the country's league. Even domestic competitions from Spain and Italy have been held in Saudi Arabia during the 2020s.

When the Ikhwan completed their conquest of the Hejaz by the end of 1925, the old cosmopolitan society of the region was uprooted. A version of Wahhabi culture was imposed there as a new compulsory social order.

In the 1994 FIFA World Cup, the Saudi Arabia team led by Jorge Solari beat both Belgium and Morocco in the group stage. It then failed to defeat Sweden in the round of 16. The country had also hosted the 1992 FIFA Confederations Cup, reaching the final and losing 1–3 to Argentina.

The Kingdom of Hejaz did not consider itself obliged to obey Ottoman laws and treaties on slavery, and was internationally known as a regional slave trade center between the wars. Between 1928 and 1931, the British consulate in Jeddah helped 81 people to be manumitted.

The Arabian ostrich was driven to extinction by hunting once rifles and, later, motor vehicles arrived. Older methods with bow and arrows and dogs had let most animals of a group escape, but rifles and cars made poaching and excessive hunting possible. One of the last sightings was a bird shot and eaten by pipeline workers in the area of Jubail in the early 1940s, and two apocryphal records from 1948 describe birds suffering the same fate. The last record, in 1966, was a dying individual found in the upper Wadi al-Hasa north of Petra.

Many slaves repatriated from the Hejaz in the 1930s had been trafficked as children. They could no longer remember where their families lived and spoke only Arabic, so they struggled to support themselves after repatriation, making authorities reluctant to receive them.
